idiom_name: class with private members owning its parts by value (std::vector<OrderLine>)
implementation_notes: C++ expresses the boundary with its own constructs: `class Order` holds `private long total_cents_; long credit_limit_; std::vector<OrderLine> lines_;`, the constructor establishes the invariant and every mutating member (add_line, remove_line) re-establishes it - the C++ Core Guidelines make this the textbook use of `class` (C.2: use class if the class has an invariant; C.9: minimize exposure of members). Parts are owned by value and copied/moved with the root, other aggregates are referenced by id (`CustomerId`), and the standard library supplies no repository, so the whole-cluster load/save plus transaction stays hand-written (a mapper over sqlite/libpq). The classic structure is directly expressed rather than replaced; the local idiom is value ownership instead of pointer graphs.
pitfalls: Returning a non-const reference or an iterator to lines_ hands callers a mutation path around the root; expose const&, a span or a copy instead.
An OrderLine must not store a pointer back to its owner: parts are owned by value inside the root, so a back-pointer becomes dangling as soon as the parent aggregate is moved or destroyed.
A public default constructor plus setters recreates the anemic model and can leave the invariant unestablished; build the aggregate through a constructor or factory that validates.

Copying the aggregate copies the whole cluster and duplicates its root identity; if roots are identity-unique, delete copy/move or define explicit clone semantics instead of treating copies as independent aggregates.
